fixes.explanation: True, and the LORD says it straight. "Every man or beast that remains in the field and is not brought inside will die when the hail comes down upon them." (Exodus 9:19) It's a heavy line, baker. The warning comes before the hail, and it begins with the LORD telling Pharaoh to give orders now to shelter his livestock and everything in the field.

Distance never comes up, friend. The text sorts the officials by one thing only. Those who feared the word of the LORD hurried to bring their servants and livestock to shelter, and those who disregarded it left them in the field (Exodus 9:20-21). The difference was how they treated the LORD's word.

That one's not it, friend. The LORD's message in this verse isn't about Moses at all. It's about Pharaoh knowing that "…there is no one like Me in all the earth." (Exodus 9:14) Moses is the one the LORD sends to deliver the message.

Wealth isn't what the LORD is talking about, friend. The verse says He raised Pharaoh up to "…display My power to you…" (Exodus 9:16) The word is power, not wealth. And it's all so that His name might be proclaimed in all the earth.

Laws are a fair guess, baker, but this verse says something else. The LORD says He raised Pharaoh up so that He might display His power. He also says He wants His name proclaimed in all the earth (Exodus 9:16). Nothing in this verse is about laws.

Thunder and lightning, baker. "So Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth." (Exodus 9:23) The LORD had told Moses to stretch out his hand toward heaven (Exodus 9:22). The text adds that the lightning kept flashing through the hail (Exodus 9:24).

Wind and darkness don't show up in this verse, friend. Here the text says the LORD sent "…thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth." (Exodus 9:23) So thunder and lightning are what came with the hail. Keep your eyes on those two.

Goshen is right, baker. "The only place where it did not hail was in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived." (Exodus 9:26) The hail struck down everything in the field throughout the land of Egypt (Exodus 9:25). Goshen was the one place it did not touch.

Canaan is a real place, friend, but this passage never mentions it. The text says the one place with no hail was "…the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived." (Exodus 9:26) That's the name to hold on to. Everywhere else in Egypt took the hail.

Midian is a good name to know, baker, but it isn't in this passage. The text names the hail-free place as "…the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived." (Exodus 9:26) Everywhere else in Egypt got hit. Goshen is the one spot that didn't.

That's what Pharaoh says, baker. "This time I have sinned," he says, and then, "The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked." (Exodus 9:27) Those are big words from him. The next verses show what he does after the storm.

Pharaoh says nothing about the LORD being far away, friend. He says, "The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked." (Exodus 9:27) He says that about the LORD, and about himself and his people. Far away never comes up.

Pharaoh asks for prayer, baker. "Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail." (Exodus 9:28) He wants the storm to end. He adds, "I will let you go…" and asks Moses and Aaron to speak to the LORD about it.

Pharaoh doesn't ask for any healing, baker. His request is short: "Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail." (Exodus 9:28) Moses answers that he will spread out his hands to the LORD (Exodus 9:29). Prayer is the request.

Not the Egyptians, baker, even with all that hail landing on their land. Moses says the thunder will cease and the hail will stop "…so that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s." (Exodus 9:29) He says the whole earth belongs to the LORD. Pharaoh is the one who needs to know it.

I wish it went that way, baker, but Moses says the opposite. "But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God." (Exodus 9:30) That word "still" matters. Pharaoh had just said he had sinned, and Moses says this right after.

Right, friend. Moses tells Pharaoh, "But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God." (Exodus 9:30) Pharaoh had just said, "The LORD is righteous," yet Moses says they still do not fear the LORD. The word "still" is the key.

True, baker. The text says "…the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops." (Exodus 9:32) The barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom, so those were destroyed (Exodus 9:31). The crop's timing made the difference.

That's what happens, baker. "When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart…" (Exodus 9:34) Only a few verses earlier he had said, "I will let you go…" (Exodus 9:28). The storm ended and so did his promise.

True, baker. The text says Pharaoh "…sinned again and hardened his heart—he and his officials." (Exodus 9:34) The officials joined him. The passage then says Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he would not let the Israelites go (Exodus 9:35).
